extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students studying real analysis and measure theory (Lebesgue measure and integration)
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter-style exposition developing outer measures, Carathéodory extension, construction of Lebesgue measure, Lebesgue integral, and key convergence theorems, with examples and exercises. Aimed at learners building rigorous measure-theoretic foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Null set and completeness (Definition 36.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A null set of a measure space (Ω, A, µ) is a set A ∈ A with µ(A) = 0. A measure space (Ω, A, µ) is complete if whenever A is a null set, then all subsets of A are in A as well (and hence null sets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition: subsets of measure-zero 'dust' should also be measurable with measure zero. The extension theorem will produce σ-algebras with this completeness property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carathéodory extension theorem for outer measures (Theorem 36.3.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If µ* is an outer measure, and A_cm is the set of µ*-measurable sets with respect to µ*, then A_cm is a σ-algebra on Ω, and the restriction µ_cm of µ* to A_cm gives a complete measure space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the principle that from an outer measure one can restrict to Carathéodory-measurable sets to get a complete measure. Note: author uses superscript cm (Carathéodory/complete).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-step construction of a measure from a pre-measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with a pre-measure µ0 on an algebra A0; form the outer measure µ* from µ0; take A_cm (µ*-measurable sets) and restrict µ* to get a complete measure µ_cm which extends µ0 on A0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives a table summarizing the steps: (Step 1) µ0 on A0 (pre-measure); (Step 2) µ* outer measure on 2^Ω; (Step 3) restriction to A_cm yields complete measure µ_cm. This is the practical recipe for producing measures like Lebesgue measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Lebesgue measure construction (Definition 36.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct Lebesgue measure on R^n by: (1) start with the algebra L0 generated by rectangular prisms and define a pre-measure λ0 on L0; (2) use Theorem 36.2.2 to get the Lebesgue outer measure λ* on 2^{R^n}, compatible with rectangular prisms; (3) apply Carathéodory to restrict to the σ-algebra L(R^n) of λ*-measurable sets and obtain the complete measure λ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resulting measure λ is the Lebesgue measure and L(R^n) is the Lebesgue σ-algebra (contains all rectangular prisms). The construction shows existence; computations then use properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for a set to have measure zero (example: Cantor set)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a set has measure zero, cover it at stage n by sets whose total measure tends to 0; e.g., Cantor set C ⊆ [0,1] has measure µ(C) ≤ (2/3)^n for every n, forcing µ(C)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General technique: show for each n you can cover the set by countably many intervals (or measurable sets) whose total measure is arbitrarily small; then the outer measure (hence measure) is zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric interpretation of Lebesgue measurability (Proposition 36.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set A ⊆ R^n is Lebesgue measurable iff for every ε>0 there is an open set U ⊃ A such that λ*(U \ A) < ε (where λ* is Lebesgue outer measure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a down-to-earth formulation: measurable sets can be approximated from outside by open sets with arbitrarily small excess outer measure. It implies open sets are measurable and hence Lebesgue σ-algebra contains the Borel σ-algebra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completion of a measure space (Definition 36.4.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given (Ω, A, µ), the completion (Ω, Ā, µ̄) is defined by Ā = {A ∪ N | A ∈ A, N ⊆ N0 for some null set N0} and µ̄(A ∪ N) = µ(A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition: extend the σ-algebra to include every subset of null sets and give such subsets measure zero. The completion is the unique extension of µ from A to Ā.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lebesgue is the completion of Borel (Theorem 36.4.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: For R^n, the Lebesgue measure is the completion of the Borel measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains the relationship: Lebesgue σ-algebra = completion of the Borel σ-algebra under the Borel measure; hence Lebesgue measurable sets strictly contain Borel sets because Borel is not complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: σ-finite definition (Definition 36.5.3) and its role
rubrics_metrics.description: A pre-measure or measure µ on Ω is σ-finite if Ω can be written as a countable union Ω = ⋃_n A_n with µ(A_n) < ∞ for each n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: σ-finiteness is often satisfied in practice (e.g., λ0 and Borel measure are σ-finite). It is a key hypothesis for uniqueness results in Carathéodory extension theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carathéodory extension theorem for pre-measures (Theorem 36.5.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let µ0 be a pre-measure on an algebra A0, and A be the σ-algebra generated by A0. Let A_cm, µ_cm be as in Theorem 36.3.4. Then (a) the restriction of µ_cm to A gives a measure µ extending µ0; (b) if µ0 was σ-finite, then µ is the unique extension of µ0 to A; (c) if µ0 was σ-finite, then µ_cm is the completion of µ, hence the unique extension of µ0 to A_cm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parts (b),(c) (uniqueness and completion) require σ-finiteness; the proof of (a) is composition of earlier theorems, while (b),(c) are more technical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicator-function integration (Step 1, Definition 37.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a measurable set A, the indicator function 1_A is defined and its integral is ∫_Ω 1_A dµ := µ(A) (possibly infinite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the base case of Lebesgue integration; integrals of indicators equal measures of sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of simple functions (Step 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a simple function s = ∑_{i=1}^n c_i 1_{A_i} with measurable A_i and nonnegative c_i (possibly +∞), define ∫ s dµ := ∑_{i=1}^n c_i µ(A_i), interpreting c_i µ(A_i)=0 when c_i = ∞ but µ(A_i)=0. The sum is independent of representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple functions (finite linear combinations of indicators) extend the indicator integral linearly and are the building blocks for nonnegative measurable functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral of nonnegative measurable functions via approximation from below (Step 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For measurable f: Ω → [0,+∞], define ∫ f dµ := sup_{0 ≤ s ≤ f} ∫ s dµ where the supremum is over simple functions s ≤ f. The integral may be +∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key method: approximate a nonnegative measurable function by an increasing net of simple functions from below; this defines the Lebesgue integral for nonnegative functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute integrability / integrable definition (Definition 37.1.2 & 37.1.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: A measurable nonnegative f is absolutely integrable (integrable) if ∫ f dµ < ∞. In general, a measurable f : Ω → [−∞,∞] is absolutely integrable if |f| is (i.e., ∫ |f| dµ < ∞).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author warns that 'integrable' is stricter than the name suggests: many measurable functions have infinite integral; absolute integrability ensures finite integral and is required for many algebraic properties (additivity, scaling for arbitrary scalars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of signed functions via positive/negative parts (Step 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For absolutely integrable f, write f^+ = max{f,0}, f^- = min{f,0}; define ∫ f dµ = ∫ |f^+| dµ − ∫ |f^-| dµ (both finite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces integration of general (signed) functions to integration of nonnegative functions and requires finiteness of both positive and negative parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning about approximation from above (Remark 37.1.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximating the integral from above by simple s ≥ f (infimum over such s) works in some bounded/finite measure settings, but fails for unbounded functions or infinite measure spaces; counterexamples given (e.g., f(x)=x^{-2} on (1,∞)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justifies why the standard Lebesgue construction uses approximation from below rather than above in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic properties of the Lebesgue integral
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and g are measurable and equal almost everywhere then integrability and integrals agree; additivity: if absolutely integrable then ∫(f+g)=∫f+∫g; scaling: ∫ cf = c∫ f for c ∈ R (when integrable); monotonicity: if f ≤ g then ∫ f ≤ ∫ g. For many of these the 'absolutely integrable' hypothesis can be dropped for nonnegative functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the algebraic and order properties used in computations; the text notes when hypotheses can be weakened (e.g., for nonnegative functions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent geometric definition of the Lebesgue integral (Section 37.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For nonnegative f, define the region under the graph R(f) = {(x,y) ∈ Ω×R : 0 ≤ y ≤ f(x)} and set ∫ f dµ := |R(f)| (measure of region).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This viewpoint interprets the integral as 'volume under the graph' and is equivalent when R(f) is measurable; it motivates some definitions and measurability conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lebesgue integral generalizes Riemann integral (Theorem 37.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : [a,b] → R is Riemann integrable (Borel measure on [a,b]), then f is Lebesgue integrable and the integrals agree: ∫_a^b f(x) dx = ∫_{[a,b]} f dµ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical upshot: Lebesgue integral extends classical Riemann theory; for computations on compact intervals with Riemann integrable functions the two coincide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper integrals as Lebesgue integrals for nonnegative continuous functions (Theorem 37.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f ≥ 0 be continuous on (a,b) (possibly a = −∞ or b = ∞). Then ∫_{(a,b)} f dµ = lim_{a'→a+, b'→b-} ∫_{a'}^{b'} f(x) dx, allowing ±∞ when not absolutely integrable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improper Riemann integrals of nonnegative functions correspond to Lebesgue integrals over the open interval, avoiding ad-hoc limiting procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fatou's lemma (Lemma 38.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For nonnegative measurable functions f_n, the function lim inf_{n→∞} f_n is measurable and ∫ lim inf_{n→∞} f_n dµ ≤ lim inf_{n→∞} ∫ f_n dµ (both sides may be +∞).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fundamental inequality controlling limit inferior of sequence integrals; the basic tool from which monotone and dominated convergence follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone convergence theorem (Corollary 38.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f_n : Ω → [0,+∞] are measurable with lim_n f_n = f and f_n(ω) ≤ f(ω) for each n, then ∫ f_n dµ → ∫ f dµ (allowing +∞).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common statement uses monotone increasing sequence f_1 ≤ f_2 ≤ ... but the text notes the weaker hypothesis f_n ≤ f for all n suffices. Proof follows from Fatou's lemma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fatou–Lebesgue inequalities (Corollary 38.4.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f_n are measurable and |f_n(ω)| ≤ g(ω) for all ω where g is absolutely integrable, then ∫ lim inf f_n ≤ lim inf ∫ f_n ≤ lim sup ∫ f_n ≤ ∫ lim sup f_n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sandwiches limits of integrals between integrals of lim inf and lim sup using Fatou applied to g ± f_n; used to prove dominated convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominated convergence theorem (Corollary 38.4.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f_n are measurable and f = lim_n f_n exists, and there is an absolutely integrable g with |f_n| ≤ |g|, then ∫ f dµ = lim_n ∫ f_n dµ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical criterion for interchanging limit and integral when a uniform integrable bound exists. Author: 'If there's only finite "space" for functions to wiggle, no anomaly can happen.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Egorov's theorem (Theorem 38.4.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If |Ω| < ∞ and f_n → f pointwise a.e., then for any ε>0 there exists U ⊆ Ω with |Ω \ U| < ε such that f_n restricted to U converges uniformly to f on U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows pointwise convergence can be upgraded to uniform convergence after removing a set of arbitrarily small measure; used to reconcile anomalies in limit/integral interchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence implies integral convergence on finite measure (Theorem 38.4.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If |Ω| < ∞ and f_n → f uniformly with each f_n integrable, then ∫ f_n dµ → ∫ f dµ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to handle the part of the domain where convergence is uniform; combined with Egorov to manage the remainder of small measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fubini and Tonelli (section reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fubini and Tonelli theorems are the main tools for swapping order of integration in product spaces (section promised, details 'TO BE WRITTEN').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tonelli handles nonnegative functions (integral of iterated equals integral over product), Fubini gives conditions for signed/absolute integrable functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topological group and locally compact abelian (LCA) group definitions (Definitions 39.1.1 & 39.1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Topological group: Hausdorff space with continuous group operation and inversion. LCA group: abelian topological group that is locally compact (every point has a compact neighborhood).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the necessary structural prerequisites to define Haar measure and Pontryagin duality; examples: finite groups (discrete), circle T (compact), R (locally compact, noncompact).

rubrics_metrics.name: Haar measure existence and properties (Theorem 39.1.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: On an LCA group G with Borel σ-algebra, there exists a Haar measure µ satisfying: translation-invariance µ(gS)=µ(S); µ(K) finite for compact K; µ(S)=inf{µ(U)|U⊇S open}; µ(U)=sup{µ(K)|K⊆U compact}. The Haar measure is unique up to positive scaling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For compact G one often normalizes µ(G)=1. These properties generalize Lebesgue measure to other topological groups and are used for Fourier analysis on groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pontryagin dual and duality theorem (Definition 39.2.1 & Theorem 39.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pontryagin dual bG := {continuous group homomorphisms ξ : G → T} (characters). The Pontryagin duality theorem: for any LCA group G there is an isomorphism G ≅ b(bG) via x ↦ (ξ ↦ ξ(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duality underlies harmonic analysis on LCA groups; examples: bZ ≅ T, bT ≅ Z, bR ≅ R, and behavior under products. Topology on bG is compact-open, not needed in detail here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters form orthonormal basis in compact case (Theorem 39.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If G is compact LCA (so bG discrete) then the characters e_ξ(x) = exp(2πi ξ(x)) for ξ ∈ bG form an orthonormal basis of L^2(G) (with Haar measure), giving expansion f = ∑_{ξ∈bG} b(ξ) e_ξ with coefficients b(ξ)=⟨f,e_ξ⟩.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generalizes Fourier series/finite Fourier transforms; sum over discrete dual bG converges in L^2 sense. Examples: finite groups, Z/nZ, circle group T.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourier inversion and transform in non-compact case (Theorem 39.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For LCA group G with Haar measure µ there exists a unique Haar measure ν on bG such that when f ∈ L^1(G) and b ∈ L^1(bG), f(x) = ∫_{bG} b(ξ) ξ(x) dν(ξ) for almost all x (for continuous f this holds for all x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides an inversion formula analogous to the Fourier transform; special cases recover continuous Fourier transform (G=R), discrete-time FT (G=Z), etc. Conditions require integrability on both sides.
